The walk builds a graph of segments
but-graph/src/init/walk — a segment is the node
A segment is a run of commits with nothing interesting in between.
now a branch lands on the middle commit:
two segments now — any recorded commit position has moved
A reference is structural here. Naming a commit can cut a node in
two — that is what split_segment and maybe_split_segments are for.
So the shape of the graph depends on which refs happened to exist,
and anything holding a segment index has to be fixed up afterwards.
The walk builds a graph of commits
but-graph/{build,walk} — a commit is the node
A commit is a commit. Segments exist only inside the builder.
now a branch lands on the middle commit:
same four commits — one row added to a table
A reference is data here. It points at a commit and changes nothing
about the structure, so there is no split and nothing to fix up.
The graph has one shape for a given history, whatever refs exist —
which is why the same build serves every view of the repository.
The graph was somebody else's type
PetGraph is an off-the-shelf graph container from crates.io. The commits
and branches live inside it, so every question goes through its API —
110 places in but-graph, across 13 files. Its habits come along:
“Petgraph traverses edges in reverse creation order, so edges are
re-added from last parent to first parent.” — post.rs

text.tspan: A full walk of the graph, to arrive back at the order git already gave.

svg.text: That is the first of the ten passes, and it buys nothing but the fix.
your types go in as parameters:
… and the container’s own index comes back out:
So the library's index becomes the project's vocabulary — 289 uses
across 32 files, escaping but-graph into seven other crates.
Two stored tables — read them like a schema
no graph library: parallel arrays, indexes and a join table
one per parent, in parent order
with row types underneath: Commit, RefInfo, Worktree (records.rs) · RefGroup,
RefLayout.groups is keyed by commit id — that is the join between the two
edge order is a column, not an artifact of insertion
These two are everything the build stores. Workspace, Stack,
StackSegment and the rest are derived from them, and stored nowhere.
you ask by commit id; the row number is a private usize that never leaves
Ten fixup traversals of the whole graph
but-graph/src/init/post.rs — 2,204 lines, run in this order
post-processing moves the entrypoint, so keep the tip
“should be first — what follows names the segments it creates”
“after all the virtual branches were added”
“better not to do this before workspaces are sorted”
every pass rewrites the previous pass's structure —
the comments are the schedule, and the schedule is the design
ten sweeps over the same graph, each undoing assumptions of the last
no pass rewrites another pass's structure — every mutation is additive
construction, or a materializer applying a decision the plan already made
so no later phase can silently undo what an earlier one decided
the build's segments are scaffolding: they author the layout and never leave the builder
four layers on the same graph — each adds, none rewrites
work out the lanes from the graph
decided inline, by post-processing passes 5 and 9
one commit, three branches on it:
“better not to do this before workspaces are sorted”

text.tspan: Two passes decide it, and they must run in that order.

svg.text: Swap them and a different branch names the commit.
Nothing records which one won, or why — the next read starts over,
and no test can assert the verdict without re-deriving everything.
one commit, three branches on it:
not integrated, and exactly one branch carrying metadata
on a stack top: metadata wins; among several, the target's own local
exactly one branch, whatever it is
A tier only answers when exactly one branch fits. A tie is not broken —
it falls through. Nothing fits at all, and the commit stays anonymous.
The winner is written into RefLayout at build time, so the next read does
not decide again — and a test can assert the verdict on its own.
WorkspaceFrame — private to init.rs, built and consumed in the same pass
Three of its eight fields are positions in this particular graph.
Hand the frame a different graph and they mean something else.
It never leaves init.rs either — workspace_frame builds it, workspace_stacks
consumes it — so no answer can be inspected apart from the lanes it produced.
WorkspaceFrame — projection/frame.rs, built once, then read-only
the floor, and what names it
Every field is a commit id or a ref name — nothing positional.
The same frame means the same thing against any graph of the repo.
And it is a published stage: built once, read by everything after,
edited by nothing — so each answer can be checked on its own.

How a commit becomes a lane
a flag seeded from the merge itself
how many stack tips reach it?
no → below the bound, not ours
identity comes from the declared partition
metadata declares one; the graph derives one; same answer, opposite ends
the integration base — nothing below is ours
the walk takes one path down — first parent, every time
one lane per walk. Tip B's commits are
reached only because the path happened
Tip C sits off the path, so it lands in no
lane at all — not shown, not addressable,
and nothing reports that it went missing.
whether a branch appears depends on the route, not on the graph
The partition engine colours the graph
the integration base — nothing below is ours
one colour per tip, painted down to the
base. No route, no order — a commit is
simply owned by whoever reaches it.
Where two colours meet above the base,
those tips are one stack — the shared
tail is stored once, not duplicated.
Tip C's colour meets nobody, so it is a
stack of its own. Nothing can be missed:
every commit above the base has an owner.
stackhood is a fact of the graph, not an outcome of the traversal
a best-effort search, run inside the same pass as everything else
the floor and the lanes are decided together, not in sequence
only the configured target prunes; a branch's own remote never does
a recording is a floor only while its ref still resolves
a missing upstream is reported rather than silently flooring nothing
what a lane is, which one it is, and what the UI finally gets
one tip, one line, no edges to store
a fork has nowhere to live —
a flat list carries no edges, so it becomes
two stacks, or one of the legs is lost
the shape the UI shows is the only shape the declaration can hold
A stack is a DAG, natively
tips converging above the base are
one stack — a graph fact, not stored shape
None for an unforked stack, so the common case costs nothing —
and today's linear lanes are derived per tip, never stored
How does the app know it is the same lane?
The lane is worked out again on every read. The id is how the app
recognises it — what you had selected, the message you are typing.
The id is not worked out at all — it is stored.
A value written into VirtualBranches.toml once, when the stack was created. Both columns read the same file.
What differs is how a freshly worked-out lane is matched to a stored id:
by scoring. Every ref in view is given a weight — the segment's own
name counts most — and the highest score wins the stored id.
A competition, so the field matters. Add a ref and the scores move;
and which ref names the segment was itself settled by the ordered
passes, so the winner can change without you touching the stack.
the same lane comes back wearing a different id
How does the app know it is the same lane?
The lane is worked out again on every read. The id is how the app
recognises it — what you had selected, the message you are typing.
The id is not worked out at all — it is stored.
A value written into VirtualBranches.toml once, when the stack was created. Both columns read the same file.
What differs is how a freshly worked-out lane is matched to a stored id:
by membership. The lane takes the id of the declared stack that owns
a branch this lane reaches. A yes-or-no question, asked once.
The branches a stack declares are input, not something the read can
move — so a ref appearing elsewhere is simply not part of the question.
Nothing declared? A fresh id, never one borrowed from a ref.
the same lane comes back wearing the same id
The UI payload is minted first, then repaired
the segment graph IS the display structure
the node IS what the UI will show
There is no assembly step, because there is nothing to assemble —
the graph already is the payload. So display decisions are baked
into the structure operations read, and pruning a lane for the
UI changes what an operation sees too.
The UI payload is assembled last
a thin partition: SegmentStack — the decided extent, nothing about looks
Vec<Stack> — for this caller, this time
Derived per call, so display cost lives at the call site. The order
is load-bearing and stated: enrich runs after hide, so it never
describes a segment that then vanishes.
And pruning is a display act. The derivation above stays total —
which is what lets operations read it pre-prune.
The same value is asked to be three things
but_graph::Workspace — worked out fresh on every read
the picture is written back to it
Arrow 2 reads the pruned picture, so what the display left out can
change where an operation anchors. Arrow 3 then saves the result —
what was drawn becomes a fact, and the next drawing starts from it.
The same value is asked to be one thing
but_graph::Workspace — worked out fresh on every read
Arrow 2 reads the total picture — everything derived, before any
pruning — so what the display hides cannot change what an operation
does. Arrow 3 is gone, so nothing it gets wrong outlives the read.
a name chosen to display becomes a durable fact
afterwards it looks exactly like something you chose
so the error does not merely show — it persists
a wrong lane is only ever shown, never authored
the declaration still holds what the last operation meant
fix the code and the next derivation is correct again
VirtualBranches.toml — the workspace metadata GitButler keeps
you run but apply A while standing on main
the view is derived — it draws lanes main and A
the write-back copies those lanes into the declaration
because that is what got drawn

text.tspan: Same result here — they part when the drawing and the request disagree.

svg.text: Anything the view pruned, renamed or could not place is recorded that way,
and no one can tell afterwards that a drawing decided it.
VirtualBranches.toml — the workspace metadata GitButler keeps
you run but apply A while standing on main
apply writes the declaration: stacks += A, and — rule 2 —
the main you were standing on
the merge is rebuilt, then the view is derived from the declaration
That is all “recording intent” means: the operation states what it did,
in the declaration, at the time it did it — before any view exists to disagree.
Rule 3 is the same move: integration mints a stand-in and says so.
Both columns are the same five-step pipeline. Every panel below is one step, shown twice — master on the left, the refactor on the right.

Ten order-dependent traversals and a write-back, against four phases that never rewrite each other and a view that only ever reads.
One thing, two vocabularies — a reference across the pipeline
the build RECORDS references and the editor MOVES them — one record on that side, three angles on this, one position store between:
— the one stored record, authored once by the build; the projection reads it, never the metadata. Its rows:
the declared partition — the one INTENT row
which branches form which stack, tip→base, with empty-chain anchors;
the stack family’s middle link: WorkspaceStack → here → SegmentStack
per commit, the ordered groups of co-located refs —
the position store the editor’s vocabulary shares
per ref: naming and emptiness verdicts, in reference-table order —
beside the entrypoint’s refs and the mutable extent
the editor is created FROM the layout — its positions are authored straight from the record — and materialization writes refs back; the next build re-records
THE EDITOR — the mutable reference, three angles
how you hold it — its row in the ref table
rows never move: stable through every rewrite; outlives removal
above · below · bottom · group top · root
the two verbs follow the model: splice what has parent entries · place what is a position
interpose a commit and the entering entries re-anchor through it (splice) — move a reference and only an ordered list makes room (place)
removal tombstones in place — record retained, indices keep resolving, revive brings it back
Two models, one measurement — the same operations against both editors
a ref-as-node needs no special machinery — until every reader pays for the machinery it doesn’t have. Rows 1–3 are the MODEL’s own costs;
row 4 is what our old IMPLEMENTATION added on top — kept apart so the argument stays honest:
REFS AS NODES — the cost disperses (master)
REFS AS POSITIONS — the cost is priced once (here)
the parents read resolves through refs
interposing refs in ancestry is what lets edge surgery move them — so a
commit’s REAL parents hide behind ref chains: a pruned DFS, per query
a commit’s parent list IS its parent list —
refs cannot appear in it by construction
connectivity doesn’t know what it connects: edge surgery around a ref
compiles without deciding what it means for the ref — disconnect never says ‘reference’
no ref edges, so decisions are unavoidable
refs live outside the edge structure: commit surgery cannot touch them,
and the only way to affect one is a named ref operation (place · splice · carry)
ancestry gains members git doesn’t have
an interposed ref — and every EMPTY branch — is an ancestry participant
with no git object; the write boundary must erase them, or corrupt the repo
commits name parents; a ref is a name plus a place —
materialization writes positions and erases nothing
…and the baseline’s own taxes (implementation, not model)
petgraph indices die on removal (normalize_selector ×18 + a remapping layer);
moves plant Step::None placeholders to keep refs anchored through surgery
tombstone-stable indices need no normalization layer, and positions don’t
live on adjacency — a move never needs a placeholder to keep refs standing

the exported-complexity bill, measured against the baseline this branch replaced: 93 → 0 raw-representation matches in callers · 433 → 0 caller-side surgery lines · 5 → 1 editor calls to move a commit
master’s move_commits implements the merge-parents rule itself and plants a placeholder node — here that rule is base_of, with one owner
